 Micron MU Stock Falls to $900 as Big Tech Spending Misses Expectations
 Micron stock has reversed to $900 after failing to reclaim $1,000, as strong memory-chip demand and SK Hynix's earnings are overshadowed by weaker-than-expected capital expenditure figures from Microsoft and Alphabet, raising concerns about future AI infrastructure spending.
 Written by: 
 Skerdian Meta 
 • 
 Thursday, October 29, 2026 
 • 
 3 min read 
 • 
 Last updated: Thursday, October 29, 2026 
 Add an article to your Reading List Register now to be able to add articles to your reading list. SIGN UP Already have an account? Sign in " aria-hidden="true"> 
 Quick overview
 Micron shares have fallen below $930 after failing to reclaim the $1,000 level, raising concerns about future AI infrastructure spending.
 Disappointing capital expenditure figures from Microsoft and Alphabet have intensified worries about the sustainability of technology infrastructure investment.
 SK Hynix's strong quarterly results support the memory-chip outlook, but Micron's performance will depend on its production capacity and market conditions.
 Increased competition from Chinese memory producers could threaten Micron's pricing and profit margins in the future.
 Micron stock has reversed to $900 after failing to reclaim $1,000, as strong memory-chip demand and SK Hynix’s earnings are overshadowed by weaker-than-expected capital expenditure figures from Microsoft and Alphabet, raising concerns about future AI infrastructure spending.
 Micron Stock Reverses Below $930
 Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) shares have lost momentum after attempting to recover toward $1,000 this week. Strong quarterly results from South Korean rival SK Hynix initially supported sentiment across the memory-chip sector, but the rally has struggled to gain traction as investors reassess the outlook for infrastructure spending.
 Micron has now fallen below $930 after failing to reclaim the psychologically important $1,000 level. The reversal reflects broader concerns that spending by major technology companies could slow, potentially affecting future revenue and earnings across the semiconductor industry.
 Microsoft and Google Spending Disappoints
 The latest quarterly results from Microsoft and Alphabet have intensified concerns about the sustainability of infrastructure investment. Alphabet reported third-quarter capital expenditure of $51.36 billion, up 114% year over year but below the market forecast of $55.78 billion. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion in capital expenditure and finance leases, compared with analysts’ expectations of $50.7 billion.
 The figures contributed to a broad technology sell-off, with Alphabet falling more than 12%, Micron declining approximately 5%, Nebius losing more than 6% and Amazon dropping nearly 3%. Oracle, CoreWeave and Riot Platforms also came under pressure.
 Although both companies continued to invest heavily, the spending shortfalls raised questions about whether infrastructure expansion will accelerate as quickly as investors previously expected.
 If major cloud providers moderate their investment plans, semiconductor suppliers could face weaker orders, slower revenue growth and pressure on valuations. This is particularly relevant for Micron, whose recent rally has benefited from expectations of sustained demand for memory used in advanced computing systems.
 SK Hynix Supports the Memory Outlook
 SK Hynix reported record quarterly revenue and operating profit, reinforcing expectations that demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) will remain strong. Management indicated that demand could exceed supply through 2030, with production effectively committed for the next three years.
 The company also announced plans to return 100 trillion won to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks.
 These developments support the broader memory-chip outlook, particularly as demand for HBM, dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) and NAND flash expands.
 However, Micron’s performance will depend on its own production capacity, product mix, pricing and customer commitments. Strong results from SK Hynix do not guarantee equivalent growth across the industry.
 Micron Stock Faces Another Technical Test
 Micron’s failure to reclaim $1,000, followed by the retreat below $930, signals renewed selling pressure. Buyers will need to stabilize the stock before another attempt at resistance becomes credible.
 The longer-term outlook remains supported by memory demand and supply constraints, but investors are increasingly focused on the sustainability of technology infrastructure spending.
 If cloud providers reduce investment, Micron could face pressure even while demand for memory continues growing. The next stage of the rally will depend on whether strong industry fundamentals can outweigh concerns about spending, competition and increasingly demanding valuations.
 MU Stock Failed at the 20 SMA 
 Micron stock  rebounded above $1,000, but the recovery faced an important technical test and we’re seeing a pullback.
 A sustained move above $1,100 would strengthen the bullish setup and could put the previous all-time high near $1,255 back into focus. However, repeated failures below $1,100 could leave the stock vulnerable to another pullback despite the strong fundamental outlook. The price has slipped below 930.
 Custom Chips and Financing Risks
 Microsoft’s development of its Maia 300 processor highlights efforts by major technology companies to improve computing efficiency through custom silicon. Although these processors still require memory, changes in hardware architecture could influence purchasing patterns and future infrastructure budgets.
 Financing conditions also present a potential challenge. Technology companies expanding data-centre capacity must demonstrate that their investments can generate sufficient returns, particularly as borrowing costs and infrastructure expenses remain significant.
 If investors become less confident in the economics of these projects, spending plans could be reassessed, affecting companies throughout the semiconductor supply chain.
 Chinese Competition Threatens Memory Pricing
 Chinese memory producer CXMT has reportedly advanced its DRAM technology and is targeting the server-memory market. Expanding capacity from Chinese competitors, alongside investment by Samsung and SK Hynix, could intensify competition over time.
 For Micron, the main risk is that supply eventually grows faster than demand, weakening memory prices and profit margins. Current supply constraints provide support, but they cannot eliminate the possibility of a future industry downturn.
 Bullish Price Targets Face a Reality Check
 D.A. Davidson raised its Micron price target to $3,000 from $2,100 while maintaining a Buy rating, citing expectations that memory supply constraints could persist through 2028. However, such ambitious targets depend on continued earnings growth and favourable pricing conditions.
 Stifel analyst Brian Chin expects DRAM shipment growth to moderate to approximately 15%–20% in 2027, potentially limiting further earnings expansion.
 Micron’s reported financial figures and guidance should be checked against its official earnings release before publication, particularly where adjusted revenue, earnings and gross-margin estimates are concerned.
